paragraphs: والثاني - انه جرى على تعظيم الذكر في خطاب الواحد بلفظ الجمع لعظم القدر كما يقول ذلك المتكلم ، قال الله تعالى " انا نحن نزلنا الذكر وانا له لحافظون " (1) وقال " ولقد خلقنا الانسان " (2) وما جرى مجراه . وروى النضر بن سمأل قال : سئل الخليل عن قوله " رب ارجعون " ففكر ثم قال : سألتموني عن شئ لا أحسنه ولا أعرف معناه ، والله أعلم ، لأنه جمع ، فاستحسن الناس منه ذلك

"The second view is that one person is addressed with a plural form to honor the greatness of the one mentioned. A speaker may say this. Allah says, “We sent down the Reminder, and We will preserve it.” He also says, “We created man,” and similar expressions. Al-Nadr ibn Shumayl reported that Khalil was asked about the words, “My Lord, send me back.” He thought for a while and said, “You asked me about something I do not know how to explain, and I do not know its meaning. Allah knows best, since it is plural.” People admired this answer."

n0015.caption: al-'Ukbari, al-Tibyan fi I'rab al-Qur'an, p274
paragraphs: ( ارْجِعُونِ ) : فيه ثلاثة أوجه : أحدها - أنه جمع على التعظيم ، كما قال تعالى : « إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ » ، وكقوله : « أَلَمْ تَرَ أَنَّ اللّه أَنْزَلَ مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً فَأَخْرَجْنا » . والثاني - أنه أراد : يا ملائكة ربّي ارجعون . والثالث - أنه دلّ بلفظ الجمع على تكرير القول فكأنه قال : ارجعني ارجعنى

"“Send me back” has three explanations. First, it uses the plural to show greatness, as Allah says, “We sent down the Reminder,” and, “Have you not seen that Allah sent water down from the sky, then We brought forth?” Second, it means, “Angels of my Lord, send me back.” Third, the plural shows repeated pleading. It is as if he said, “Send me back, send me back.”"

n0019.caption: al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v3, p42
paragraphs: يخاطبون النبي - صلى اللّه عليه - وحده ، وهو كقوله : « يا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِذا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّساءَ » (1) في كثير من كلام العرب ، أن تجمع العرب فعل الواحد ، منه قول اللّه ﷿ : « قالَ رَبِّ ارْجِعُونِ

They address the Prophet alone. It is like His saying, “O Prophet, when you divorce women” (1), in much Arab speech, where the Arabs use the plural form of the verb for one person. Among this is God's saying, “He said, ‘My Lord, send me back.’”

n0022.caption: al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v2, p13
paragraphs: بِأَعْيُنِنا وَوَحْيِنا ) [ 37 ] كقوله ( ارْجِعُونِ (7) ) يخرج على الجمع ومعناه واحد على ما فسّرت لك من قوله ( بَلْ نَظُنُّكُمْ كاذِبِينَ ) لنوح وحده

“Under Our eyes and by Our revelation” [37], like His saying, “Return” [7], is expressed in the plural although its meaning is singular, according to what I explained to you concerning His saying, “Rather, we think you are liars,” which was addressed to Noah alone.

n0025.caption: al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v2, p241
paragraphs: فجعل الفعل كأنه لجميع (3) وإنما دعا ربه . فهذا ممّا جرى على
So he made the verb as though it were for all (3), though he only called upon his Lord. This is among what occurred according to

n0026.caption: al-Farra, Ma'ani al-Qur'an, v2, p242, continued on the following page
paragraphs: ما وصف اللّه به نفسه من قوله ( وقد خلقناك (1) من قبل ) في غير مكان من القرآن . فجرى هذا على ذلك
what God described Himself with in His saying, “And We created you (1) before,” in another place of the Quran. This follows that.

n0030.caption: Abu al-Salah al-Halabi, Taqrib al-Ma'arif, p188
paragraphs: لأن العبارة عن الواحد بلفظ الجمع على جهة التعظيم ظاهر في العربية . وكون علي ﵇ فقيرا غير معلوم
"Arabic clearly uses plural wording for one person to show honor. It is unknown whether Ali was poor."

n0032.caption: Abu Ali, in Ma'rifa al-Imam, v5, p24
paragraphs: قال الشيخ أبو عليّ : قال جار الله (2) : إنّما جيء به على لفظ الجمع - وإن كان السبب فيه رجلًا واحداً - ليرغّب الناس في مثل فعله ، ولينبّه أنّ سجيّة المؤمن يجب أن تكون على هذه الغاية من الحرص على البرّ والإحسان . ثمّ قال الشيخ أبو عليّ : وأقول : قد اشتهر في اللغة العبارة عن الواحد بلفظ الجمع للتعظيم ، فلا يحتاج إلى الاستدلال عليه (من قِبل جار الله) .

"Shaykh Abu Ali said that Jar Allah said, "It came in the plural form, though one man caused its revelation, to encourage people to do the same. It also teaches that a believer should be deeply eager for goodness and kindness." Shaykh Abu Ali then said, "Arabic commonly uses plural wording for one person to show honor, so there is no need to prove the point against Jar Allah.""

n0034.caption: al-Mar'ashi, Sharh Ihqaq al-Haqq, v3, p587
paragraphs: نزلنا عنه ، لكن لم لا يجوز أن يكون المراد منه عليا ﵇ ، والواحد قد يعبر عنه بلفظ الجمع ، على سبيل التعظيم كقوله تعالى : إنا أنزلناه في ليلة القدر (1) ، وقال في حق علي ﵇ : والذين يقيمون الصلاة ويؤتون الزكاة وهم راكعون (2)

"We accept that, yet why could it not mean Ali? One person may be described with a plural form to show honor, as Allah says, “We sent it down on the Night of Decree.” He also says about Ali, “Those who establish prayer, give alms, and bow down.”"

n0040.caption: Imru' al-Qays, in Nashwan al-Himyari, Shams al-'Ulum, v3, p287
paragraphs: نحن الملوك وأبناء الملوك لنا * مُلكٌ به عاش هذا الناسُ أحقابا
nahnu al-muluku wa-abna'u al-muluki lana / mulkun bihi 'asha hadha al-nasu ahqaba
"We are kings, sons of kings. Our rule has kept these people alive for ages."

n0043.caption: Lisan al-'Arab, v6, p229, root n-d-s
paragraphs: ونَجْرانُ : مدينة بناحية اليمن ؛ يريد أَنهم أَغاروا عليهم عند الصباح ، وتميم بن مر منصوب على الاختصاص لقوله نحن صبحنا ؛ كقول آخر : نَحْنُ بَنِي ضَبَّةَ أَصْحابُ الجَمَل وكقول النبي ، صلى اللّه عليه وسلم : نَحْنُ مَعاشِرَ الأَنْبِياء لا نَرِثُ ولا نُورَثُ
nahnu sabahna ... nahnu bani Dabbata ashabu al-jamal ... nahnu ma'ashira al-anbiya'i la narithu wa-la nurath

"Najran is a city near Yemen. He means that they raided its people at dawn. Tamim ibn Murr is in the accusative case for special mention in the phrase, “We raided at dawn.” Another poet said, “We, the sons of Dubba, are the people of the Camel.” The Prophet also said, “We, the community of prophets, neither inherit nor leave inheritance.”"

n0047.caption: al-Razi, Tafsir al-Razi, v6, p216
paragraphs: القول الثاني : أن المراد بهذه الآية محمد ﵇ ، لأنه هو المفصل على الكل ، وإنما قال : (ورفع بعضهم درجات) على سبيل التنبيه والرمز كمن فعل فعلا عظيما فيقال له : من فعل هذا فيقول أحدكم أو بعضكم ويريد به نفسه ، ويكون ذلك أفخم من التصريح به ، وسئل الحطيئة عن أشعر الناس ، فذكر زهيراً والنابغة ، ثم قال : ولو شئت لذكرت الثالث أراد نفسه ، ولو قال : ولو شئت لذكرت نفسي لم يبق فيه فخامة

"The second view is that this verse means Muhammad, since he is the one favored above all others. It says, “He raised some of them in ranks,” as a hint and an allusion. A person may do something great and be asked, “Who did this?” He may answer, “One of you,” or “Some of you,” while meaning himself. This sounds grander than naming himself directly. Al-Hutay'ah was asked who was the greatest poet. He named Zuhayr and al-Nabighah, then said, “If I wished, I could name the third.” He meant himself. Had he said, “If I wished, I could name myself,” the grandeur would have disappeared."

n0050.caption: al-Jurjani, al-Hashiya 'ala al-Kashshaf, p63
paragraphs: وأشار بقوله (وقد التفت امرؤ القيس) إلى نوع رابع هو الانتقال من التكلم إلى الخطاب في ليلك واقتصر على هذه الأربعة لأنها أكثر الأنواع وأشهرها ... أما في علم المعاني فباعتبار كونه على خلاف مقتضي الظاهر . وأما في البيان فباعتبار أنه إيراد لمعنى واحد في طرق مختلفة الدلالة عليه جلاء وخلفاء وبهذين الاعتبارين يفيد الكلام حسنا ذاتيا للبلاغة . أما في البديع فمن حيث إن فيه جمعا بين صور متقابلة في معنى واحد فكان من المحسنات المعنوية ... فيكون ليلك التفاتا من التكلم إلى الخطاب

"His words, “Imru al-Qays shifted,” point to a fourth type, the change from speaking in the first person to addressing someone directly in “your night.” He mentioned these four because they are the most common and famous types. In the science of meanings, this shift differs from what the situation normally requires. In rhetoric, it expresses one meaning through different ways that make it clearer and more vivid. These two aspects give speech its own beauty and eloquence. In literary embellishment, it joins opposite forms within one meaning, so it is a type of meaningful embellishment. Thus, “your night” shifts from the first person to direct address."

n0057.caption: Ibn Shahrashub, Mutashabih al-Qur'an, v2, p272
paragraphs: لفظ جمع يراد به الواحد - ما كانَ لِلْمُشْرِكِينَ أَنْ يَعْمُرُوا مَساجِدَ اللَّهِ يعني المسجد الحرام - إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يُنادُونَكَ وهو رجل نادى يا محمد إن مدحي زين وإن شتمي شين - وَلْيَشْهَدْ عَذابَهُما طائِفَةٌ مِنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ الطائفة خرجت من حيز الواحد ودخلت في آخر - وفي التفسير واحد واثنان فما فوقهما - بِمَ يَرْجِعُ الْمُرْسَلُونَ وهو واحد يدل عليه قوله ارْجِعْ إِلَيْهِمْ ... أما قوله لمالك أَلْقِيا فِي جَهَنَّمَ ففي أخبار أهل البيت ع إن الخطاب للنبي ص وأمير المؤمنين ع وقال المبرد هذا فعل مثنى للتأكيد كأنه قال ألق ألق

"A plural word may mean one person. "The idolaters must not maintain Allah's mosques" means the Sacred Mosque. "Those who call out to you" refers to one man who called, "Muhammad, my praise is beauty and my insult is disgrace." "Let a group of believers witness their punishment" leaves the register of the single one and enters another. In the commentary it can be one, two, or more. "See what the messengers return with" refers to one person, as shown by the words, "Return to them." As for His words to Malik, "Cast both of you into Hell," reports from the People of the House say that Allah addressed the Prophet and the Commander of the Faithful. Al-Mubarrad said this is a dual verb used for emphasis, as if He said, "Cast, cast.""

n0060.caption: Manaqib Ibn Shahrashub, in Bihar al-Anwar, v16, p336
paragraphs: مناقب ابن شهرآشوب : كان له اثنان وعشرون خاصية : كان أحسن الخلائق : " الذي خلقك فسواك (4) " وأجملهم : " لقد خلقنا الانسان في أحسن تقويم (5) "

"From Manaqib Ibn Shahrashub. He had twenty-two special qualities. He was the finest of all creatures, “He created you and formed you well.” He was also the most beautiful of them, “We created man in the finest form.”"

n0062.caption: Qur'an 82:7 and 95:4, as cited in Bihar al-Anwar, v16, p336
paragraphs: الذي خلقك فسواك ... لقد خلقنا الانسان في أحسن تقويم
alladhi khalaqaka fa-sawwaka ... laqad khalaqna al-insana fi ahsani taqwim
"He created you and shaped you. We created the human being in the finest form."

n0064.caption: Qur'an 38:71-72, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v3, p151, with Qur'an 66:12, Majma' al-Bahrayn, v4, p116
paragraphs: إِذْ قالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلائِكَةِ إِنِّي خالِقٌ بَشَراً مِنْ طِينٍ . فَإِذا سَوَّيْتُهُ وَنَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِنْ رُوحِي ... ونفخنا فيه من روحنا
idh qala rabbuka lil-mala'ikati inni khaliqun basharan min tin. fa-idha sawwaytuhu wa-nafakhtu fihi min ruhi ... wa-nafakhna fihi min ruhina
"When your Lord said to the angels, "I am creating a human being from clay. When I have formed him and breathed into him of My spirit..." And We breathed into him of Our spirit."

n0068.caption: Qur'an 2:34, as cited in al-Kafi, v1, p474
paragraphs: وإذ قلنا للملائكة اسجدوا لآدم فسجدوا إلا إبليس أبى
wa-idh qulna lil-mala'ikati usjudu li-adama fa-sajadu illa Iblis. aba
"When We said to the angels, "Bow down before Adam," they bowed down except Iblis. He refused."

n0071.caption: Qur'an 19:64, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v2, p294
paragraphs: وَما نَتَنَزَّلُ إِلَّا بِأَمْرِ رَبِّكَ لَهُ ما بَيْنَ أَيْدِينا وَما خَلْفَنا وَما بَيْنَ ذلِكَ وَما كانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّا (64)
wa-ma natanazzalu illa bi-amri rabbika. lahu ma bayna aydina wa-ma khalfana wa-ma bayna dhalika. wa-ma kana rabbuka nasiyya
"We descend only by your Lord's command. To Him belongs what lies before us, what lies behind us, and what lies between them. Your Lord never forgets."

n0073.caption: Qur'an 33:56, as printed in Majma' al-Bayan, v8, p179
paragraphs: إن الله وملائكته يصلون على النبي ... يا أيها الذين آمنوا صلوا عليه وسلموا تسليما
inna Allaha wa-mala'ikatahu yusalluna 'ala al-nabi. ya ayyuha alladhina amanu sallu 'alayhi wa-sallimu taslima
"Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. You who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace."

n0075.caption: Qur'an 97:1-4, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v3, p574
paragraphs: إِنَّا أَنْزَلْناهُ فِي لَيْلَةِ الْقَدْرِ (1) وَما أَدْراكَ ما لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ (2) لَيْلَةُ الْقَدْرِ خَيْرٌ مِنْ أَلْفِ شَهْرٍ (3) تَنَزَّلُ الْمَلائِكَةُ وَالرُّوحُ فِيها بِإِذْنِ رَبِّهِمْ مِنْ كُلِّ أَمْرٍ (4)
inna anzalnahu fi laylati al-qadr. wa-ma adraka ma laylatu al-qadr. laylatu al-qadri khayrun min alfi shahr. tanazzalu al-mala'ikatu wa-al-ruhu fiha bi-idhni rabbihim min kulli amr

"We sent it down on the Night of Decree. What will make you understand what the Night of Decree is? The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months. The angels and the Spirit descend in it by their Lord's permission with every command."

n0077.caption: Qur'an 50:16, al-Jadwal fi I'rab al-Qur'an, v30, p52
paragraphs: وَلَقَدْ خَلَقْنَا الْإِنْسانَ وَنَعْلَمُ ما تُوَسْوِسُ بِهِ نَفْسُهُ وَنَحْنُ أَقْرَبُ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ حَبْلِ الْوَرِيدِ
wa-laqad khalaqna al-insana wa-na'lamu ma tuwaswisu bihi nafsuh. wa-nahnu aqrabu ilayhi min habli al-warid
"We created the human being, and We know what his soul whispers to him. We are nearer to him than his jugular vein."

n0079.caption: Qur'an 15:9, as printed in al-Burhan fi Tafsir al-Qur'an, v3, p397
paragraphs: إِنَّا نَحْنُ نَزَّلْنَا الذِّكْرَ وإِنَّا لَه لَحافِظُونَ
inna nahnu nazzalna al-dhikra wa-inna lahu la-hafizun
"We have sent down the Reminder, and We will surely preserve it."

n0085.caption: Qur'an 51:47-51, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v3, p328
paragraphs: وَالسَّماءَ بَنَيْناها بِأَيْدٍ وَإِنَّا لَمُوسِعُونَ (47) وَالْأَرْضَ فَرَشْناها فَنِعْمَ الْماهِدُونَ (48) وَمِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ خَلَقْنا زَوْجَيْنِ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَذَكَّرُونَ (49) فَفِرُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ إِنِّي لَكُمْ مِنْهُ نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ (50) وَلا تَجْعَلُوا مَعَ اللَّهِ إِلهاً آخَرَ إِنِّي لَكُمْ مِنْهُ نَذِيرٌ مُبِينٌ (51)

wa-al-sama'a banaynaha bi-aydin wa-inna la-musi'un. wa-al-arda farashnaha fa-ni'ma al-mahidun. wa-min kulli shay'in khalaqna zawjayni la'allakum tadhakkarun. fa-firru ila Allahi inni lakum minhu nadhirun mubin. wa-la taj'alu ma'a Allahi ilahan akhara inni lakum minhu nadhirun mubin

"We built the heaven with strength, and We are surely expanding it. We spread out the earth, and how excellent are We at preparing it. We created every thing in pairs, so that you may remember. Flee to Allah. I am a clear warner to you from Him. Do not set up another god beside Allah. I am a clear warner to you from Him."

n0087.caption: al-Tabrisi, Majma' al-Bayan, v9, p267
paragraphs: المعنى : ( والسماء بنيناها بأيد ) تقديره وبنينا السماء بنيناها بقوة ، عن ابن عباس ومجاهد وابن زيد وقتادة أي : خلقناها ورفعناها ، على حسن نظامها ( وإنا لموسعون ) أي قادرون على خلق ما هو أعظم منها ... ( والأرض فرشناها ) ... ( فنعم الماهدون ) نحن إذ فعلنا ذلك للمنافع ومصالح العباد ، لا لجر نفع ، ولا لدفع ضرر

"The meaning of “We built the sky with strength” is, We built the sky with power. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, and Qatadah said this means that We created it and raised it in a fine order. “We are fully able” means that We can create what is greater than it. “We spread out the earth.” “How excellent are We at preparing it.” We did this for the benefit and welfare of people. We did not do it to gain benefit or prevent harm."

n0088.caption: al-Tabrisi, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v3, p329
paragraphs: ( وَالْأَرْضَ فَرَشْناها ) أي بسطناها ومهدناها لمنافع العباد وخلقنا من كل شيء صنفين مثل الليل والنهار ، والأرض والسماء ، والشمس والقمر ، والجن والإنس ، والبر والبحر ، وقيل : الزوجين الذكر والأنثى لكي تعلموا أن خالق هذه الأزواج واحد لا يشبهه أحد

"We spread out the earth and prepared it for people's needs. We created everything in pairs, such as night and day, earth and sky, sun and moon, jinn and humans, and land and sea. It is also said that the pair means male and female, so that you may know that the Creator of these pairs is One and that nothing resembles Him."

n0090.caption: al-Tabataba'i, al-Mizan, v18, p381
paragraphs: ( بيان ) تشير الآيات إلى عدة من آيات الله الدالة على وحدانيته في الربوبية ورجوع أمر التدبير في الأرض والسماء والناس وأرزاقهم إليه ... والاستنتاج الآتي في آخر هذه الآيات في قوله : ( ففروا إلى الله - إلى أن قال - ولا تجعلوا مع الله إلها آخر ) الآية ، يشهد على أن سوق هذه الآيات والدلائل لاثبات وحدانيته تعالى في الربوبية

"Explanation. The verses point to several signs of Allah that prove He alone governs all things. He directs the earth, the sky, people, and their provision. The conclusion at the end says, "Flee to Allah," then, "Do not set up another god with Allah." This shows that these verses and proofs establish that Allah alone rules and governs."

n0093.caption: Tafsir al-Qummi, v2, p448
paragraphs: سورة الاخلاص مكية آياتها خمس ط (بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم قل هو الله أحد) اي هو الله الأحد وكان سبب نزولها ان اليهود جاءت إلى رسول الله ﵌ فقالت : ما نسب ربك ؟ فأنزل الله (قل هو الله أحد الله الصمد لم يلد ولم يولد ولم يكن له كفوا أحد) ومعنى قوله : أحد أحدي النعت كما قال رسول الله ﵌ : نور لا ظلام فيه وعلم لا جهل فيه وقوله : الصمد ، اي الذي لا مدخل فيه وقوله : لم يلد ، اي لم يحدث ولم يولد ولم يكن له كفوا أحد ، قال : لا له كفو ولا شبيه ولا شريك ولا ظهير ولا معين .

"Surat al-Ikhlas was revealed in Mecca. It has five verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Say, 'He is Allah, the One.' The Jews came to the Messenger of Allah and asked, "What is your Lord's lineage?" Then Allah revealed, "Say, He is Allah, the One, Allah, the Everlasting Refuge. He did not beget, and He was not born. No one is equal to Him." Ahad means that His attributes are unique. The Messenger of Allah said, "He is a light free of darkness and knowledge free of ignorance." Al-Samad means the One with no opening within Him. "He did not beget" means that He did not bring anything into existence. "He was not born, and no one is equal to Him." He has no equal, no likeness, no partner, no supporter, and no helper."

n0100.caption: al-Mashhadi, Kanz al-Daqa'iq, v1, p118
paragraphs: وفي إيراد « إياك » دون « إياه » ، كما هو مقتضى الظاهر ، التفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب . ومن النكتة الخاصة ، في الالتفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب ، في هذا المقام ، بعد اشتماله على فائدة عامة ، من جهة المتكلم ، وهي التصرف والافتنان في وجود الكلام واظهار القدرة عليها ، ومن جهة المخاطب ، وهي تطرية نشاطه في سماع الكلام ، وايقاظه للإصغاء إليه . أنه لما قيل : « إياك » بدل « إياه » ، فقد نزل الغائب بواسطة أوصافه المذكورة التي أوجب تميزه وانكشافه ، حتى صار كأنه تبدل خفاء غيبته ، بجلاء حضوره ، منزلة المخاطب في التمييز والظهور

"The use of iyyaka carries the speech from referring to someone absent into directly addressing Him. This shift has a general benefit. For the speaker, it shows skill and variety in expression. For the hearer, it renews attention and wakes the listener to hear carefully. Here it has a further purpose. The word iyyaka brings the One previously spoken of through His qualities into the position of one directly addressed. Those qualities distinguished Him and made Him known. The hiddenness of His absence became as clear as His presence. He therefore became like one directly addressed in clarity and distinction."

n0103.caption: al-Tabataba'i, al-Mizan, v3, p377
paragraphs: وأعلم أن في الآيات موارد من الالتفات من الغيبة إلى الخطاب ومن خطاب الجمع إلى خطاب المفرد وبالعكس وفيها موارد من وضع الظاهر موضع الضمير كتكرر لفظ الجلالة في عدة مواضع والنكتة في الجميع ظاهرة للمتأمل

"Know that these verses include shifts from speaking about Allah to speaking directly to Him. They also shift between addressing many people and addressing one person. In some places, they use an explicit noun where a pronoun would usually appear, such as repeating the name Allah several times. A thoughtful reader can see the purpose of all these expressions."

n0105.caption: al-Mazandarani, Sharh Usul al-Kafi, v1, p122
paragraphs: (فقال : إذا قيل لهم) الضمير للناس في قوله تعالى : (يا أيها الناس كلوا مما في الأرض حلالاً طيباً ولا تتبعوا خطوات الشيطان) على سبيل الالتفات من الخطاب إلى الغيبة للتنبيه على بعدهم عن رتبة الخطاب بسبب سلوكهم طريق التقليد

"In the words, "When it is said to them," the pronoun refers to the people in Allah's words, "People, eat what is lawful and good on the earth. Do not follow Satan's footsteps." The speech shifts from directly addressing them to speaking about them. This alerts us that following imitation has kept them far from the rank of direct address."

n0106.caption: al-Mazandarani, Sharh Usul al-Kafi, v3, p204
paragraphs: (الذي لا يدركنا الغالي) الموصول صفة للنمط الأوسط وإفراده باعتبار اللّفظ والأصل أن يقول لا يدركه بالضمير للموصول إلاّ أنّه أتى بضمير المتكلّم من باب الالتفات من الغيبة إلى التكلّم للتصريح بالمقصود كما في قول أمير المؤمنين (﵇) : «أنا الّذي سمّتني أمي حيدرة»

"In “the extremist cannot grasp us,” the relative pronoun describes the middle pattern. It is singular because of its wording. The original wording would be “cannot grasp him,” using a pronoun that refers back to the relative pronoun. The verse brings the first-person pronoun, a shift from the third person to the first. It states the intended meaning plainly, as Amir al-Muminin said, “I am the one my mother named Haydara.”"

n0109.caption: al-Iskandari, al-Insaf, v2, p174
paragraphs: ثم التفات من التكلم إلى الغيبة بقوله - واعلموا أنكم غير معجزي الله وأن الله - وأصله واعلموا أنكم غير معجزي وأنى ، وفي هذا الالتفات بعد الالتفات الأول افتنان في أساليب البلاغة وتفخيم للشأن وتعظيم للأمر ... وكل هذا من حسنات الفصاحة

"Then the speech turns from "We" to speaking about Allah by name in, "Know that you cannot escape Allah, and that Allah..." Its original form was, "Know that you cannot escape Me, and that I..." This shift, after the first shift, shows variety in eloquent expression. It gives the matter greater weight and importance. All of this belongs to the beauties of eloquence."

n0113.caption: al-Tabrisi's gloss, in Bihar al-Anwar, v18, p173
paragraphs: وقال في قوله تعالى : " إنه لقول رسول كريم " أي إن القرآن قول رسول كريم على ربه وهو جبرئيل (﵇) ، وهو كلام الله أنزله على لسانه ، ثم وصف جبرئيل فقال : " ذي قوة " أي فيما كلف وامر به من العلم والعمل وتبليغ الرسالة ... " أمين " على وحي الله ورسالاته إلى أنبيائه

"Regarding Allah's words, "It is truly the word of a noble messenger," he said that the Quran is the word brought by a noble messenger before his Lord, who is Jibril. It is Allah's speech, which He sent down through Jibril. Allah then describes Jibril, "Possessing strength," meaning strength in the knowledge, actions, and delivery of the message entrusted to him. "Trustworthy," meaning trustworthy with Allah's revelation and His messages to His prophets."

n0117.caption: from al-Hasan, in Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v1, p118
paragraphs: روي عن الحسن أن سائلا سأل النبي ( ص ) أقريب ربنا فنناجيه أم بعيد فنناديه ؟ فنزلت الآية
"Hasan reported that a questioner asked the Prophet, "Is our Lord near, so we may speak quietly to Him, or far, so we must call out to Him?" Then the verse came down."

n0121.caption: Qur'an 2:186, Mukhtasar Majma' al-Bayan, v1, p118
paragraphs: وَإِذا سَأَلَكَ عِبادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ أُجِيبُ دَعْوَةَ الدَّاعِ إِذا دَعانِ فَلْيَسْتَجِيبُوا لِي وَلْيُؤْمِنُوا بِي لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْشُدُونَ
wa-idha sa'alaka 'ibadi 'anni fa-inni qarib. ujibu da'wata al-da'i idha da'an. fa-l-yastajibu li wa-l-yu'minu bi la'allahum yarshudun
"When My servants ask you about Me, I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls Me. Let them answer Me and believe in Me, so that they may be rightly guided."

n0123.caption: al-Saduq, 'Uyun Akhbar al-Rida ﵇, v1, p269
paragraphs: حدثنا محمد بن القاسم المفسر الأسترآبادي ﵁ قال : حدثنا يوسف بن محمد بن زياد وعلي بن محمد بن سيار عن أبويهما عن الحسن بن علي عن أبيه علي بن محمد عن أبيه محمد بن علي عن أبيه الرضا علي بن موسى عن أبيه موسى بن جعفر عن أبيه جعفر بن محمد عن أبيه محمد بن علي عن أبيه علي بن الحسين عن أبيه الحسين بن علي عن أبيه أمير المؤمنين علي بن أبي طالب ﵈ قال : قال رسول الله : قال الله ﷿ : قسمت فاتحه الكتاب بيني وبين عبدي فنصفها لي ونصفها لعبدي ولعبدي ما سال إذا قال العبد (بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم) قال الله جل جلاله : بدأ عبدي باسمي وحق على أن أتمم له أموره وأبارك له في أحواله فإذا قال : (الحمد لله رب العالمين) قال الله ﷿ : حمدني عبدي وعلم أن النعم التي له من عندي وان البلايا التي دفعت عنه فبطولي أشهدكم انى أضيف له إلى نعم الدنيا نعم الآخرة ... فإذا قال : (إياك نعبد) قال الله ﷿ : صدق عبدي إياي يعبد ... فإذا قال : (اهدنا الصراط المستقيم) إلى آخر السورة قال الله ﷿ : هذا لعبدي ولعبدي ما سال

"Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, the commentator from Astarabad, reported from Yusuf ibn Muhammad ibn Ziyad and Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sayyar, from their fathers, from Hasan ibn Ali, from his father Ali ibn Muhammad, from his father Muhammad ibn Ali, from his father al-Rida Ali ibn Musa, from his father Musa ibn Jafar, from his father Jafar ibn Muhammad, from his father Muhammad ibn Ali, from his father Ali ibn al-Husayn, from his father al-Husayn ibn Ali, from his father Amir al-Muminin Ali ibn Abi Talib. The Messenger of Allah said that Allah said, "I divided the Opening of the Book between Me and My servant. Half belongs to Me, and half belongs to My servant. My servant will receive what he asks for."

n0129.caption: Imam al-Sadiq ﵇, al-Kafi, v2, p515
paragraphs: علي بن إبراهيم ، عن أبيه ، عن صفوان بن يحيى ، عن إسحاق بن عمار ، عن بعض أصحابه ، عن أبي عبد الله (﵇) قال : إن لله ﷿ ثلاث ساعات في الليل وثلاث ساعات في النهار يمجد فيهن نفسه ... يقول : إني أنا الله رب العالمين ، إني أنا الله العلي العظيم ، إني أنا الله العزيز الحكيم ، إني أنا الله الغفور الرحيم ، إني أنا الله الرحمن الرحيم ، إني أنا الله مالك يوم الدين ، إني أنا الله لم أزل ولا أزال ... إني أنا الله الواحد الصمد ... إني أنا الله الكبير المتعال . قال : ثم قال أبو عبد الله (﵇) من عنده ، والكبرياء رداءه فمن نازعه شيئا من ذلك أكبه الله في النار ، ثم قال : ما من عبد مؤمن يدعو بهن مقبلا قلبه إلى الله ﷿ إلا قضى حاجته

"Ali ibn Ibrahim reported from his father, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, from one of his companions, that Abu Abd Allah said, "Allah has three hours in the night and three hours in the day when He praises Himself. He says, 'I am Allah, Lord of all worlds. I am Allah, the Most High, the Great. I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. I am Allah, the Forgiving, the Merciful. I am Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. I am Allah, Master of the Day of Judgment. I am Allah. I have always existed, and I will always exist. I am Allah, the One, the Eternal Refuge. I am Allah, the Great, the Most High.'"

n0132.caption: Abu al-Hasan ﵇, al-Kafi, v2, p489
paragraphs: محمد بن يحيى ، عن أحمد بن محمد بن عيسى ، عن أحمد بن محمد بن أبي نصر قال : قلت لأبي الحسن (﵇) : جعلت فداك إني قد سألت الله حاجة منذ كذا وكذا سنة وقد دخل قلبي من إبطائها شئ ، فقال : يا أحمد إياك والشيطان أن يكون له عليك سبيل حتى يقنطك ... فكن بالله أوثق فإنك على موعد من الله ، أليس الله ﷿ يقول : " وإذا سألك عبادي عني فإني قريب أجيب دعوة الداع دعان (1) " وقال : " لا تقنطوا من رحمة الله (2) " وقال : " والله يعدكم مغفرة منه وفضلا (3) " فكن بالله ﷿ أوثق منك بغيره

"Muhammad ibn Yahya reported from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, who said, "I said to Abu al-Hasan, 'May I be your ransom. I have asked Allah for something for many years, and its delay has troubled my heart.'"

n0135.caption: Imam al-Sadiq ﵇, relaying Ali ibn al-Husayn ﵇, al-Kafi, v1, p296
paragraphs: وبهذا الاسناد ، عن أبي عبد الله ﵇ قال : كان علي بن الحسين صلوات الله عليه يقول : " إنا أنزلناه في ليلة القدر " صدق الله ﷿ أنزل الله القرآن في ليلة القدر " وما أدراك ما ليلة القدر " قال رسول الله ﵌ : لا أدري ، قال الله ﷿ " ليلة القدر خير من الف شهر " ليس فيها ليلة القدر ، قال لرسول الله ﵌ : وهل تدري لم هي خير من الف شهر ؟ قال لا ، قال : لأنها تنزل فيها الملائكة والروح بإذن ربهم من كل أمر ، وإذا أذن الله ﷿ بشئ فقد رضيه " سلام هي حتى مطلع الفجر " يقول : تسلم عليك يا محمد ملائكتي وروحي بسلامي من أول ما يهبطون إلى مطلع الفجر

"Through the same chain, Abu Abd Allah reported that Ali ibn al-Husayn would say, "Allah spoke the truth when He said, 'We sent it down on the Night of Decree.' Allah sent down the Quran on the Night of Decree. 'What will make you know what the Night of Decree is?'"

n0142.caption: Imam al-Kazim ﵇, al-Kafi, v1, p474
paragraphs: الحسين بن محمد ، عن معلى بن محمد ، عمن أخبره ، عن علي بن جعفر قال سمعت أبا الحسن ﵇ يقول : لما رأى رسول الله ﵌ تيما وعديا وبني أمية يركبون منبره أفظعه ، فأنزل الله ﵎ قرآنا يتأسى به : " وإذ قلنا للملائكة اسجدوا لآدم فسجدوا إلا إبليس أبى (5) " ثم أوحى إليه يا محمد إني أمرت فلم اطع فلا تجزع أنت إذا أمرت فلم تطع في وصيك

"Husayn ibn Muhammad reported from Mulla ibn Muhammad, from someone who informed him, from Ali ibn Jafar, who said, "I heard Abu al-Hasan say, 'When the Messenger of Allah saw Taym, Adi, and Banu Umayyah climbing his pulpit, it distressed him. Allah sent down Quran to comfort him with, "When We said to the angels, 'Bow down before Adam,' they bowed down, except Iblis. He refused." Then Allah revealed to him, "Muhammad, I commanded and was disobeyed. Do not grieve when you command people regarding your successor and they disobey you."'""

n0148.caption: al-Razi, Tafsir al-Razi, v28, p225
paragraphs: المسألة الرابعة : إذا كان المقصود إثبات التوحيد ، فكيف قال : ( بنيناها ) ولم يقل بنيتها أو بناها الله ؟ نقول قوله : ( بنينا ) أدل على عدم الشريك في التصرف والاستبداد وقوله بنيتها يمكن أن يكون فيه تشريك ... فإذن علم أن المراد جمع التعظيم وأفاد النص عظمته ، فالعظمة أنفى للشريك فثبت أن قوله : ( بنيناها ) أدل على نفي الشريك من بنيتها وبناها الله . فإن قيل : لم قلت : إن الجمع يدل على التعظيم ؟ قلنا الجواب من الوجهين . الأول : أن الكلام على قدر فهم السامع ، والسامع هو الإنسان ، والإنسان يقيس الشاهد على الغائب ، فإن الكبير عندهم من يفعل الشيء بجنده وخدمه ولا يباشر بنفسه ، فيقول الملك فعلنا أي فعله عبادنا بأمرنا ويكون في ذلك تعظيم ، فكذلك في حق الغائب

"Fourth question. If the aim is to establish God's oneness, why does He say, "We built it," and not, "I built it," or, "God built it"? We answer, "We built it" more clearly shows that no one shares His control or independent power. "I built it" may suggest a partnership. The intended meaning is therefore the plural of majesty. The wording shows His greatness. His greatness excludes any partner. Thus, "We built it" more clearly denies a partner than "I built it" or "God built it."

n0152.caption: Abu Hayyan, al-Bahr al-Muhit, v7, p346
paragraphs: والمخصوص بالمدح محذوف تقديره : فلنعم المجيبون نحن ، وجاء بصيغة الجمع للعظمة والكبرياء لقوله : (فَقَدَرْنَا فَنِعْمَ الْقَادِرُونَ)

"The one praised is omitted. Its meaning is, "How excellent are We in answering." He used the plural form to show majesty and greatness, as in His words, "We determined, and how excellent are We at determining.""

n0153.caption: al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, v12, p96
paragraphs: والجمع للعظمة والكبرياء وفيه من تعظيم أمر الإجابة ما فيه ؛ وأخرج ابن مردويه عن عائشة رضي اللّه تعالى عنها قالت : «كان النبي صلّى اللّه عليه وسلم إذا صلى في بيتي فمر بهذه الآية وَلَقَدْ نادانا نُوحٌ فَلَنِعْمَ الْمُجِيبُونَ قال : صدقت ربنا أنت أقرب من دعا وأقرب من بغى فنعم المدعو ونعم المعطي ونعم المسؤول ونعم المولى أنت ربنا ونعم النصير»

"The plural expresses majesty and greatness, and it gives the act of answering great importance. Ibn Marduyah reported from Aisha that whenever the Prophet prayed in her home and passed this verse, "Noah called upon Us, and how excellent are We in answering," he said, "You have spoken the truth, our Lord. You are nearer than the one who calls upon You, and nearer than the one who transgresses. How excellent are You to call upon, how excellent are You to give, how excellent are You to ask, how excellent are You as Master. You are our Lord, and how excellent are You as Helper.""

n0155.caption: al-Sha'rawi, Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, v5, p232
paragraphs: فالأسلوب القرآني حين يأتي ب «إني» يشير إلى وحدة الذات ، وحين يأتي ب «إنا» يشير إلى تجمع صفات الكمال ... لذلك لا بد من ضمير التعظيم الذي يقول فيه النحويون : إن «نحن» و «نا» للمعظم نفسه . وقد عظم الحق نفسه ؛ لأن الأمر هنا حشد صفات يتطلبها إيجاد الكون والقيام على أمر الكون . ... فسبحان رب فوق كل مظنة تعالى جلالا أن يحاط بذاته / إذا قال «إني» ذاك وحدة قدسه وإن قال «إنّا» ذاك حشد صفاته

"When the Quranic style says, "I," it points to the oneness of the Divine Being. When it says, "We," it points to the gathering of perfect qualities. Therefore, the pronoun of majesty is necessary. Grammarians say that "We" and "Us" refer to the One who is great. The Truth has declared His own greatness because creating the universe and governing it require a gathering of attributes.

n0162.caption: Genesis 1:26, Westminster Leningrad Codex, King James Version
paragraphs: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר אֱלֹהִ֔ים נַֽעֲשֶׂ֥ה אָדָ֛ם בְּצַלְמֵ֖נוּ כִּדְמוּתֵ֑נוּ
va-yomer elohim na'aseh adam be-tsalmenu ki-demutenu
"And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness."

n0163.caption: Deuteronomy 6:4, Westminster Leningrad Codex, King James Version
paragraphs: שְׁמַ֖ע יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל יְהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵ֖ינוּ יְהוָ֥ה ׀ אֶחָֽד
shema yisra'el YHWH elohenu YHWH echad
"Hear, O Israel, the LORD our God is one LORD."

The Argument Under Examination

The charge comes in two forms, and both travel widely. The first asks it as arithmetic. Your book says We created you, We sent down the Reminder, We built the heaven. A plural speaker is plural, so who are the others helping Allah? The second asks it as confusion. The same book keeps moving between We, He, and I, sometimes inside one passage, and a speaker who knows who he is does not keep changing his own pronouns.

Both forms assume one thing, that an Arabic pronoun counts its referents the way an English pronoun does. It does not. Arabic has a standing plural of majesty, a we that one exalted speaker says of himself alone. The rule is printed in the grammar books, alive in the poets, and used by the Quran itself for single referents of no theological weight at all. When the Quran means that others act alongside Allah, it names them. When it wants the nearness of answer, it drops the say-command and speaks as I. When it describes the Lord for the servant to learn of Him, it says He. One Speaker, and many rooms of speech.
Conclusion

The We carries majesty and never number, and no helper hides inside it, because the plural of majesty is ordinary Arabic and the Quran names its co-agents when it has them. The shifts of person follow design, because iltifat is a named device the Imams themselves use. The charge survives only by reading an Arabic pronoun as an English census, and that method convicts Genesis before it reaches the sura of the Reminder.

1. The Grammar and the Lexicon

The charge rests on one grammatical assumption, that a pronoun counts its referents. Arabic breaks that assumption before the Quran is even opened. The language has a plural of majesty, nahnu, a we that one exalted speaker says of himself alone. The rule is printed in the grammar books with the Quran's own We as the textbook example.

Contested words. The charge reads nahnu, the Arabic we, as a count of speakers, and the person-shifts as a change of speaker. The grammarians, the lexicon's witnesses, the poets, and the Quran's own usage fix nahnu as register, and the shifts as a named device with named purposes.

The school's senior classical commentator states the rule first. The speech of one speaker can run in the plural form for greatness of station, and he says this is simply how speakers of Arabic talk. His parallel is the charge's own target, the doubled We of the Reminder verse (Qur'an 15:9), and the We of man's creation (Qur'an 23:12). The report he relays records both edges. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, a founder of Arabic grammar, was asked about the plural of the dying soul's plea in Qur'an 23:99, send them back, addressed to the one God. He declined to force a parse and said he does not know its analysis, because it is a plural, and the people of his circle found the reserve good. Al-Farra answered him within a generation. The founder's own stated reason is form-side, because it is a plural, and the Kufan school answered him within a generation. Al-Tusi's statement is the tradition resolving what the founder left open, the plural of rank named where he paused. It runs in both directions, a creature addressing the one God in the plural and God speaking of Himself in it. Neither direction carries number.

Fourth question. If the aim is to establish God's oneness, why does He say, "We built it," and not, "I built it," or, "God built it"? We answer, "We built it" more clearly shows that no one shares His control or independent power. "I built it" may suggest a partnership. The intended meaning is therefore the plural of majesty. The wording shows His greatness. His greatness excludes any partner. Thus, "We built it" more clearly denies a partner than "I built it" or "God built it." If someone asks, "Why do you say that the plural shows majesty?" We answer in two ways. First, speech follows what the listener can understand. The listener is human. People compare what they see with what they cannot see. They consider great a ruler who acts through his armies and servants without acting personally. A king says, "We did it," meaning, "Our servants did it by our command." This gives him majesty. The same applies to the Unseen.

The king says we did, meaning that his servants did it at his command, and there is magnification in it. If the king's we means his servants, does Allah's We mean His angels? Wherever creatures act, the book names them, and named creatures under command are the retinue, worshippers who descend by permission, not helpers sharing the act's rank. It confessed one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made, God from God, of the same substance as the Father. The synagogue's classic commentary reads the plural another way, as God consulting his heavenly court (Rashi on Genesis 1:26), and that reading is as old as the dispute.

The comparison runs on four named tests. First, what each view asks a believer to accept about God. Second, whether each reading coheres with its own scripture. Third, which reading fits the words themselves. Fourth, which demands less of the text.

On the first test, each reading must square with its own scripture's monotheism, and both books hold the pair, plural forms and strict oneness, without dissolving either. On the second, the Quranic reading is a rule of the language the book speaks, settled by dictionaries, grammars, and usage. The Trinitarian reading of Genesis reads the fourth-century creed back into Hebrew written a millennium before it.

On the third test, the words themselves. Augustine argues from the plural pronouns to plurality of persons, so the number of the pronoun is the load-bearing point, and the Hebrew grammar gives it no such freight. The noun of God stands under singular agreement, and Deuteronomy above shows a plural noun of God standing under one LORD, with nobody reading the morphology as a census. Genesis 1:26's verb is plural in form, like the Arabic nahnu, and English answers that case with its own royal we. The queen says we are, and never we is, one speaker under plural agreement. On the fourth test, the plural of majesty needs no extra persons and no creed to import them, while the Trinitarian reading needs Nicaea to decide what the us means.

The strongest remaining objection is the retinue reading. Read the king's we as executors hidden inside the pronoun, and the divine We becomes Allah with his angels as his retinue. The book names the retinue wherever it acts, and the named retinue are creatures under command, worshippers who descend by permission and salute the Prophet, which is not the plurality the charge wants. The charge needs helpers of the divine act who share the act's rank. The book gives creatures who carry out the act of the One. The grammar of majesty and the rule that names its co-agents together leave the retinue standing only as what has already been named, creatures under command, with nothing between creature and Creator inside the pronoun.

The sophisticated form of the Christian reading does not rest on the pronoun at all. It reads Genesis through John's prologue, all things made through him, and through Paul's by him all things were created. That reading carries its agent into the Hebrew from outside it, and a Christian holds the agent's book to be inside his canon, so the four tests cannot reach his form of the case. That is the honest boundary. The pronoun charge is the popular form, and it is the form answered here. The creedal form rests on the creed, and between the two readings the majesty reading is the one the language itself carries. A method that convicts the Quran's We convicts Genesis first, and applied with one standard it convicts neither.
Glossary of Key Terms
nahnu. the Arabic we. When Allah says nahnu, the plural is the Arabic plural of majesty, one exalted speaker, and the book names any creature who shares the act.
iltifat. the turn, a named device of Arabic eloquence in which a speaker shifts grammatical person mid-passage, from speaking about Allah to addressing Him, or from first person to third.
the say-verses. the verses that open with qul, say, where Allah composes the Prophet's exact words to recite, the visible grammar of the relay.
qudsi report. a sacred report in which Allah speaks in the first person, relayed by the Prophet and transmitted through the Imams.
riwa'i. the transmitted reports, the hadith layer, as the school calls it.
the Reminder. al-dhikr, the Quran's own name for itself in Qur'an 15:9.
mufassirun. the Quran commentators.
the wilaya verse. Qur'an 5:55, whose plural verbs the school reads of one man, Ali, giving zakat while bowing.

blocks.text: The charge comes in two forms, and both travel widely. The first asks it as arithmetic. Your book says We created you, We sent down the Reminder, We built the heaven. A plural speaker is plural, so who are the others helping Allah? The second asks it as confusion. The same book keeps moving between We, He, and I, sometimes inside one passage, and a speaker who knows who he is does not keep changing his own pronouns.
blocks.observation: Meta sweep verified: "The charge comes in two forms, and both" opens on content with no roadmap or announcement.

blocks.text: Both forms assume one thing, that an Arabic pronoun counts its referents the way an English pronoun does. It does not. Arabic has a standing plural of majesty, a we that one exalted speaker says of himself alone. The rule is printed in the grammar books, alive in the poets, and used by the Quran itself for single referents of no theological weight at all. When the Quran means that others act alongside Allah, it names them. When it wants the nearness of answer, it drops the say-command and speaks as I. When it describes the Lord for the servant to learn of Him, it says He. One Speaker, and many rooms of speech.

blocks.text: The We carries majesty and never number, and no helper hides inside it, because the plural of majesty is ordinary Arabic and the Quran names its co-agents when it has them. The shifts of person follow design, because iltifat is a named device the Imams themselves use. The charge survives only by reading an Arabic pronoun as an English census, and that method convicts Genesis before it reaches the sura of the Reminder.

blocks.observation: Meta sweep verified: "1. The Grammar and the Lexicon" opens on content with no roadmap or announcement.

blocks.text: The charge rests on one grammatical assumption, that a pronoun counts its referents. Arabic breaks that assumption before the Quran is even opened. The language has a plural of majesty, nahnu, a we that one exalted speaker says of himself alone. The rule is printed in the grammar books with the Quran's own We as the textbook example.
blocks.observation: Meta sweep verified: "The charge rests on one grammatical assumption, that" opens on content with no roadmap or announcement.

blocks.text: Contested words. The charge reads nahnu, the Arabic we, as a count of speakers, and the person-shifts as a change of speaker. The grammarians, the lexicon's witnesses, the poets, and the Quran's own usage fix nahnu as register, and the shifts as a named device with named purposes.
blocks.observation: Meta sweep verified: "Contested words. The charge reads nahnu, the Arabic" opens on content with no roadmap or announcement.

blocks.text: The school's senior classical commentator states the rule first. The speech of one speaker can run in the plural form for greatness of station, and he says this is simply how speakers of Arabic talk. His parallel is the charge's own target, the doubled We of the Reminder verse (Qur'an 15:9), and the We of man's creation (Qur'an 23:12). The report he relays records both edges. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, a founder of Arabic grammar, was asked about the plural of the dying soul's plea in Qur'an 23:99, send them back, addressed to the one God. He declined to force a parse and said he does not know its analysis, because it is a plural, and the people of his circle found the reserve good. Al-Farra answered him within a generation. The founder's own stated reason is form-side, because it is a plural, and the Kufan school answered him within a generation. Al-Tusi's statement is the tradition resolving what the founder left open, the plural of rank named where he paused. It runs in both directions, a creature addressing the one God in the plural and God speaking of Himself in it. Neither direction carries number.

blocks.text: Al-Farra, who died in 207 and took the Kufan school from the generation of al-Kisa'i, the Kufan master reader of the Quran, is commenting on Qur'an 44:36. There the opponents address the Prophet ﷺ alone. He says the plural verb for the one addressee is ordinary Arabic, and his parallel is inside the Quran itself. The sura of divorce opens, O Prophet, when you divorce, with the singular title of honor and the plural verb in one clause (Qur'an 65:1). The dying soul's send me back (Qur'an 23:99) is, he says, of the same kind. The later tafsir commonly reads the plural of 65:1 as a turn to the community with the Prophet; al-Farra's reading is the Kufan school's own. The book itself addresses one man in the plural and reports one man addressing his one Lord in the plural.

blocks.text: The second view is that this verse means Muhammad, since he is the one favored above all others. It says, “He raised some of them in ranks,” as a hint and an allusion. A person may do something great and be asked, “Who did this?” He may answer, “One of you,” or “Some of you,” while meaning himself. This sounds grander than naming himself directly. Al-Hutay'ah was asked who was the greatest poet. He named Zuhayr and al-Nabighah, then said, “If I wished, I could name the third.” He meant himself. Had he said, “If I wished, I could name myself,” the grandeur would have disappeared.

blocks.text: His words, “Imru al-Qays shifted,” point to a fourth type, the change from speaking in the first person to addressing someone directly in “your night.” He mentioned these four because they are the most common and famous types. In the science of meanings, this shift differs from what the situation normally requires. In rhetoric, it expresses one meaning through different ways that make it clearer and more vivid. These two aspects give speech its own beauty and eloquence. In literary embellishment, it joins opposite forms within one meaning, so it is a type of meaningful embellishment. Thus, “your night” shifts from the first person to direct address.

blocks.text: The poets practiced the shifts long before the Quran, and the rhetoricians came later and named what the poets had been doing. And the question of codification cuts both ways. A rule read out of the Quran would explain the Quran perfectly and nothing else. This rule explains the poets, the kings, the dying soul's plea, and the book at once, and a rule that explains all of them was already in the language. The demand for a pre-Islamic king saying we of himself alone should also be measured against the opponent's own ground. The only divine plurals his canon carries are in-scripture, Genesis 1:26 and its companions. The only in-scripture plural-for-one the Quran needs is likewise inside the book, the dying soul's plea and the single Prophet addressed in the plural. A bar that the opponent's own evidence does not clear is not a bar the Quran has to clear.

blocks.text: A plural word may mean one person. "The idolaters must not maintain Allah's mosques" means the Sacred Mosque. "Those who call out to you" refers to one man who called, "Muhammad, my praise is beauty and my insult is disgrace." "Let a group of believers witness their punishment" leaves the register of the single one and enters another. In the commentary it can be one, two, or more. "See what the messengers return with" refers to one person, as shown by the words, "Return to them." As for His words to Malik, "Cast both of you into Hell," reports from the People of the House say that Allah addressed the Prophet and the Commander of the Faithful. Al-Mubarrad said this is a dual verb used for emphasis, as if He said, "Cast, cast."

blocks.text: In Qur'an 19:64 the we is the angels' own voice, the Prophet the addressee, and their Lord named in the third person with His command as their only warrant. Where the mufassirun, the Quran commentators, have heard the angels sharing in an act, they pointed to the verses that name them. Those verses are the descent by permission (Qur'an 97:4) and the wings (Qur'an 35:1). The plural of majesty is never left carrying them unmarked. The book tells its speakers apart by naming them, and this verse is where it does so.

blocks.text: Surat al-Ikhlas was revealed in Mecca. It has five verses. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Say, 'He is Allah, the One.' The Jews came to the Messenger of Allah and asked, "What is your Lord's lineage?" Then Allah revealed, "Say, He is Allah, the One, Allah, the Everlasting Refuge. He did not beget, and He was not born. No one is equal to Him." Ahad means that His attributes are unique. The Messenger of Allah said, "He is a light free of darkness and knowledge free of ignorance." Al-Samad means the One with no opening within Him. "He did not beget" means that He did not bring anything into existence. "He was not born, and no one is equal to Him." He has no equal, no likeness, no partner, no supporter, and no helper.

The device itself the rhetoricians named, and the school's commentary assigns its purposes verse by verse.

blocks.text: The use of iyyaka carries the speech from referring to someone absent into directly addressing Him. This shift has a general benefit. For the speaker, it shows skill and variety in expression. For the hearer, it renews attention and wakes the listener to hear carefully. Here it has a further purpose. The word iyyaka brings the One previously spoken of through His qualities into the position of one directly addressed. Those qualities distinguished Him and made Him known. The hiddenness of His absence became as clear as His presence. He therefore became like one directly addressed in clarity and distinction.

blocks.text: When the book says He, Allah speaks, and the carriers are named. The clearest statement is the gloss on 69:40, the word of a noble messenger, and it is Allah's speech placed on his tongue. Add the grammar of the say-verses, where Allah composes the Prophet's exact words, and the architecture is complete. Allah speaks, Jibril carries to the Prophet's heart, the Prophet recites, and each layer is grammatically visible in the book. Third-person self-presentation plus named relay is the book's standing design. A questioner asked the Prophet whether the Lord is near, that they should whisper, or far, that they should call out. The answer came down without the say-command, and the Lord answered the questioner in His own person.

blocks.text: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim, the commentator from Astarabad, reported from Yusuf ibn Muhammad ibn Ziyad and Ali ibn Muhammad ibn Sayyar, from their fathers, from Hasan ibn Ali, from his father Ali ibn Muhammad, from his father Muhammad ibn Ali, from his father al-Rida Ali ibn Musa, from his father Musa ibn Jafar, from his father Jafar ibn Muhammad, from his father Muhammad ibn Ali, from his father Ali ibn al-Husayn, from his father al-Husayn ibn Ali, from his father Amir al-Muminin Ali ibn Abi Talib. The Messenger of Allah said that Allah said, "I divided the Opening of the Book between Me and My servant. Half belongs to Me, and half belongs to My servant. My servant will receive what he asks for." When the servant says, "In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," Allah says, "My servant began with My name. I will complete his affairs and bless his circumstances." When the servant says, "Praise belongs to Allah, Lord of all worlds," Allah says, "My servant praised Me. He knows that every blessing he has comes from Me, and that I turned away the trials that missed him through My grace. I call you to witness that I will add the blessings of the next life to his blessings in this life." When the servant says, "You alone we worship," Allah says, "My servant has spoken truly. He worships Me alone." When the servant says, "Guide us on the straight path," until the end of the chapter, Allah says, "This belongs to My servant. My servant will receive what he asks for."

blocks.text: Ali ibn Ibrahim reported from his father, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, from one of his companions, that Abu Abd Allah said, "Allah has three hours in the night and three hours in the day when He praises Himself. He says, 'I am Allah, Lord of all worlds. I am Allah, the Most High, the Great. I am Allah, the Mighty, the Wise. I am Allah, the Forgiving, the Merciful. I am Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. I am Allah, Master of the Day of Judgment. I am Allah. I have always existed, and I will always exist. I am Allah, the One, the Eternal Refuge. I am Allah, the Great, the Most High.'" Abu Abd Allah continued, "Greatness belongs to Allah, and majesty is His cloak. Allah will throw into the Fire anyone who disputes any part of that with Him. No believing servant calls upon Allah with these words while turning his heart toward Him except that Allah fulfills his need."

blocks.text: Muhammad ibn Yahya reported from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr, who said, "I said to Abu al-Hasan, 'May I be your ransom. I have asked Allah for something for many years, and its delay has troubled my heart.'" Abu al-Hasan replied, "Ahmad, beware of Satan. Do not let him gain power over you and make you lose hope. Trust Allah more deeply. Allah has promised you. Does Allah not say, 'When My servants ask you about Me, I am near. I answer the call of the caller when he calls upon Me'? He also says, 'Do not lose hope in Allah's mercy.' He says, 'Allah promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty.' Trust Allah more than you trust anyone else."

blocks.text: Through the same chain, Abu Abd Allah reported that Ali ibn al-Husayn would say, "Allah spoke the truth when He said, 'We sent it down on the Night of Decree.' Allah sent down the Quran on the Night of Decree. 'What will make you know what the Night of Decree is?'" The Messenger of Allah said, "I do not know." Allah said, "The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months." No Night of Decree exists within those thousand months. Allah asked the Messenger of Allah, "Do you know why it is better than a thousand months?" The Messenger of Allah replied, "No." Allah said, "The angels and the Spirit descend in it, by their Lord's permission, with every command. When Allah permits something, He is pleased with it. 'Peace it is until the rising of dawn.' My angels and My Spirit greet you, Muhammad, with My peace from the moment they descend until dawn rises."

blocks.text: Fourth question. If the aim is to establish God's oneness, why does He say, "We built it," and not, "I built it," or, "God built it"? We answer, "We built it" more clearly shows that no one shares His control or independent power. "I built it" may suggest a partnership. The intended meaning is therefore the plural of majesty. The wording shows His greatness. His greatness excludes any partner. Thus, "We built it" more clearly denies a partner than "I built it" or "God built it." If someone asks, "Why do you say that the plural shows majesty?" We answer in two ways. First, speech follows what the listener can understand. The listener is human. People compare what they see with what they cannot see. They consider great a ruler who acts through his armies and servants without acting personally. A king says, "We did it," meaning, "Our servants did it by our command." This gives him majesty. The same applies to the Unseen.

blocks.text: The king says we did, meaning that his servants did it at his command, and there is magnification in it. If the king's we means his servants, does Allah's We mean His angels? Wherever creatures act, the book names them, and named creatures under command are the retinue, worshippers who descend by permission, not helpers sharing the act's rank. The custom explains the register. Wherever creatures act, the book names them. The verdict is not al-Razi's alone.

blocks.text: Isaiah's call carries the I and the us in one sentence, the Lord sending and a we commissioning, the canon's own person-shift at the throne. Rashi's court reading carries these verses by naming the addressees, and the court reading is plurality without Trinity, creatures around the throne, which is the Quran's own picture wherever its book names the court. One more line closes the door between the readings. Plurality is not triunity. Even a reading that won every pronoun would still have to build exactly three co-eternal persons of one substance out of the verb's number, and no verb carries that freight.

blocks.text: Augustine reads the Genesis plural as the Son's presence in creation, in On the Trinity I.7.14. His argument is that were the Father alone to have made man without the Son, the plural of Genesis 1:26 would never have been written. The Council of Nicaea in 325 confessed one God the Father Almighty, maker of all things. It confessed one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made, God from God, of the same substance as the Father. The synagogue's classic commentary reads the plural another way, as God consulting his heavenly court (Rashi on Genesis 1:26), and that reading is as old as the dispute.
blocks.observation: Meta sweep verified: "Augustine reads the Genesis plural as the Son's" opens on content with no roadmap or announcement.

blocks.text: The comparison runs on four named tests. First, what each view asks a believer to accept about God. Second, whether each reading coheres with its own scripture. Third, which reading fits the words themselves. Fourth, which demands less of the text.
blocks.observation: Meta sweep verified: "The comparison runs on four named tests. First," opens on content with no roadmap or announcement.

blocks.text: On the first test, each reading must square with its own scripture's monotheism, and both books hold the pair, plural forms and strict oneness, without dissolving either. On the second, the Quranic reading is a rule of the language the book speaks, settled by dictionaries, grammars, and usage. The Trinitarian reading of Genesis reads the fourth-century creed back into Hebrew written a millennium before it.
blocks.observation: Meta sweep verified: "On the first test, each reading must square" opens on content with no roadmap or announcement.

blocks.text: On the third test, the words themselves. Augustine argues from the plural pronouns to plurality of persons, so the number of the pronoun is the load-bearing point, and the Hebrew grammar gives it no such freight. The noun of God stands under singular agreement, and Deuteronomy above shows a plural noun of God standing under one LORD, with nobody reading the morphology as a census. Genesis 1:26's verb is plural in form, like the Arabic nahnu, and English answers that case with its own royal we. The queen says we are, and never we is, one speaker under plural agreement. On the fourth test, the plural of majesty needs no extra persons and no creed to import them, while the Trinitarian reading needs Nicaea to decide what the us means.
blocks.observation: Meta sweep verified: "On the third test, the words themselves. Augustine" opens on content with no roadmap or announcement.

blocks.text: The strongest remaining objection is the retinue reading. Read the king's we as executors hidden inside the pronoun, and the divine We becomes Allah with his angels as his retinue. The book names the retinue wherever it acts, and the named retinue are creatures under command, worshippers who descend by permission and salute the Prophet, which is not the plurality the charge wants. The charge needs helpers of the divine act who share the act's rank. The book gives creatures who carry out the act of the One. The grammar of majesty and the rule that names its co-agents together leave the retinue standing only as what has already been named, creatures under command, with nothing between creature and Creator inside the pronoun.
blocks.observation: Meta sweep verified: "The strongest remaining objection is the retinue reading." opens on content with no roadmap or announcement.

blocks.text: The sophisticated form of the Christian reading does not rest on the pronoun at all. It reads Genesis through John's prologue, all things made through him, and through Paul's by him all things were created. That reading carries its agent into the Hebrew from outside it, and a Christian holds the agent's book to be inside his canon, so the four tests cannot reach his form of the case. That is the honest boundary. The pronoun charge is the popular form, and it is the form answered here. The creedal form rests on the creed, and between the two readings the majesty reading is the one the language itself carries. A method that convicts the Quran's We convicts Genesis first, and applied with one standard it convicts neither.

advisors.response:
Contrarian seat report — `quran-we-he-i.html`, whole page read (1,092 lines), new exhibits spot-verified against the al-Farra text on the titan corpus.

**New defects introduced by the revision (concrete, fixable)**

1. **Locus error, exhibit 2 (verified).** The "Our eyes" gloss is labeled Qur'an 54:14 in the premise card, prose, and Facts table. Corpus check (Ma'ani al-Qur'an v2, p13): the gloss sits inside al-Farra's run on Surat Hud — markers [30] [35] [36] then the quoted `بِأَعْيُنِنا وَوَحْيِنا [ 37 ]`. The phrase *with وحينا* is 11:37 ("make the ark under Our eyes and by Our revelation"); 54:14 has only `بِأَعْيُنِنَا`. The prose "The ark of Noah floating under Our eyes and by Our inspiration (Qur'an 54:14)" also splices 54:14's floating onto 11:37's phrase, and renders وحينا two ways ("revelation" in the translation, "inspiration" in the prose). Fix: relabel 11:37, "built under Our eyes and by Our inspiration," one rendering.
2. **Locus error, exhibit 3/4 (verified).** "We created you before" is glossed as Qur'an 20:115 in the premise card and prose ("Locus: ... with 20:115, across a page boundary"; "the divine We created you before (Qur'an 20:115)"). 20:115 is `وَلَقَدْ عَهِدْنَا إِلَىٰ آدَمَ`. The phrase `وقد خلقناك من قبل ولم تك شيئا` is the Kufan qira'a of **19:9** (corpus: Fath al-Bayan v4 p278, "وقرأ سائر الكوفيين وقد خلقناك ولم تك شيئا"). The claim itself survives (first-person-plural divine speech, exactly as used) — only the verse number is wrong. Note: the revision brief supplied the same wrong locus, so the error propagated from the plan.
3. **Bisected quotation reads badly.** The p241/p242 sentence is split into two premise cards and two blockquotes; the first translation ends mid-preposition ("This is among what occurred according to"). Fix: one card citing "v2, pp241-242" with the joined sentence and a page-boundary ellipsis note. Also the fragment translation "So **He** made the verb as though it were for all" capitalizes a subject the Arabic leaves ambiguous and most naturally takes as the dying speaker — lowercase.
4. **Verdict attribution overreach.** "That was the charge the polemic itself chose when it likened the Quran's We to Genesis 1:26." Nothing in the article documents the polemic making that likeness; section 8 constructs the Genesis parallel itself ("the method... has a home address"). A hostile reader simply denies ever running it and claims the creedal case was always primary, dissolving the "concession." Fix: qualify ("the popular polemic, as it commonly does, likens...") or quote the opponent text that makes the likeness.
5. **Facts table under-registers the new block.** Four new quotations, two Facts rows (v3 p42, v2 p13). The 23:99↔"We created you" equation (pp241-242) is unregistered.
6. Minor: "The grammar books cited so far were written in the fifth and sixth centuries" — al-'Ukbari d.616 is seventh-century AH. Say "fifth century and after."

**Residual escape hatches (not defects, hostile-reader inventory)**

- **All grammatical attestation is post-Quran.** Al-Farra (d.207) is still ~150 years after revelation; a hostile reader can refuse 2nd/3rd-century grammar as evidence of pre-Quranic usage. The article anticipates this twice (§2's "codification cuts both ways"; the block's closer on teachers "who carried the language of the age before the book"), and the poets + 23:99-in-book argument is the right answer. Residual but well-met.
- **The al-Khalil reframe.** "Paused over the parse, not the referent" is an inference layered on `لا أعرف معناه... لأنه جمع` — the quote itself lets a hostile reader say "the founder said he did not know its meaning." The article prints the quote honestly and answers it with al-Farra; acceptable, but the inference should not be presented as the report's content.
- **The angels reading of 23:99.** The claim card says al-'Ukbari has it "stated and outweighed"; the quoted text lists three views with no visible tarjih. Soften to "stated among three alternatives" or quote the weighing.
- **65:1.** Standard tafsir reads the plural as a turn to the community, not plural-of-majesty for one addressee. The exhibit is faithful to al-Farra and claims no consensus; a hostile reader can still invoke the majority parse. No fix needed beyond awareness.
- **Retinue inversion.** Since Jibril is the named carrier of the descent (2:97), a hostile reader can say the We's act *is* executed by a named creature — blurring "carries majesty and never number." §7-8 answer this (named creatures under permission are not the plurality the charge wants); the line holds.

Redundancy check: the three al-Farra exhibits re-tread 23:99 a third and fourth time after al-Tusi and al-'Ukbari, but the payoff (dating, and the creature-plural/divine-We equation) is genuinely new and the prose marks the purpose. Not redundancy; only exhibit 3's presentation (defect 3) is weak. Insertion-point flow is otherwise clean: the al-Khalil paragraph absorbs the reframe, the "Back in the fifth-century layer" signpost recovers the thread, and `#tab1-farra` is anchored and linked from the Facts table.

**Scores**

# Council verdict — quran-we-he-i.html (post-revision)

## Seat 1 — First Principles: the three hatches

**(a) Creedal form (John 1:3 / Col 1:16 beyond the four tests): closed as an escape from this article's verdict; not refuted, and honestly not claimed to be.** Section 8 already states the boundary plainly: "the four tests cannot reach his form of the case. That is the honest boundary." The Final Verdict then converts the retreat into a concession: "A reader who abandons the pronoun and retreats to the creed... has conceded the pronoun case. That was the charge the polemic itself chose when it likened the Quran's We to Genesis 1:26." That is sound scoping, not overreach: the page's stated thesis is the pronoun charge in its two forms ("does We mean others help Allah" and "why the shifts"), so retreating to Nicaea abandons the load-bearing premise of that charge. What remains is a different article (the creedal case on its own ground), which the page correctly says "must be argued from there." Within the declared scope, genuinely closed; no pronoun article can close it further.

**(b) Pre-Islamic attestation of a strictly solitary royal we: materially weakened, with the residual honestly conceded rather than hidden.** The al-Farra chain does three distinct things. First, it dates the rule to d. 207 AH at the founding grammatical layer, so the rule is no longer a fifth-century Shi'i harmonization meeting the reader first at al-Tusi. Second, it exhibits the rule *inside the Quran at a theologically neutral verse*: 65:1, "the singular title of honor and the plural verb in one clause," which answers the circularity objection the page itself states best ("A rule read out of the Quran would explain the Quran perfectly and nothing else," line 545). Third, al-Farra glosses the divine Our itself ("plural in form and singular in meaning") and equates the creature's plural of 23:99 with "We created you before" (20:115), so the divine-We-as-majesty reading is attested at the earliest layer in both directions. Residual, and the page concedes it: the strictly solitary pre-Islamic we is still exhibited only through post-Quranic compilation ("Every human we on exhibit gathers rank around a speaker standing with his people"), and al-Farra is still two centuries after the book. The escape now requires discounting all post-Quranic grammar, which destroys the opponent's own Arabic philology. Weakened to a tolled position, not fully closed.

**(c) al-Khalil's reserve: closed as far as dated texts allow.** The reframe rests on checkable chronology: "The reserve predates the rule, and the rule answers the reserve. The founder paused over the parse, not the referent, and his own Kufan succession answered him within a generation" (line 427). Al-Khalil d. 170 AH, al-Farra d. 207 AH through al-Kisa'i's circle; "within a generation" is accurate. The reserve is scoped by al-Khalil's own stated reason ("because it is plural"). One wording outruns the quote slightly (finding F3 below). No textual escape remains; only the skeptic who discounts the whole grammatical tradition, which is hatch (b)'s tolled position again.

**What remains overall:** the token-ambiguity objection (Seat 2) and the strictly-solitary-we concession. Both are standing residuals of evidence, not defects of inference.

## Seat 2 — Reasoning

**The al-Farra chain is multi-link, not a single generalization.** "The Arabs use the plural verb for one person" (v3 p42) alone would *not* license "the divine We carries no number"; that is a second-person address construction generalizing to first person. But the page does not rest there: the 11:37 gloss is a direct statement on the divine first-person Our ("expressed in the plural while its meaning is singular"), and the 23:99 ↔ 20:115 equation puts creature-to-God plural and God's own We under one rule in one running comment. The chain holds.

**The 65:1 parallel holds as internal usage on al-Farra's stated reading, and that is its one dependency.** Correctly attributed ("The earliest commentary on the grammar of these verses counts no second speaker," line 466), but the mainstream alternative reading of talaqtum (the Prophet together with the community, the ruling generalized) is unengaged; on that reading the plural counts real referents and the neutral-exhibit force drops. One sentence acknowledging and weighing it would close the gap.

**The scope-catcher is an argument, not a device.** It is a dilemma: either the pronoun carries number, and then the four tests apply and "a method that convicts the Quran's We convicts Genesis first"; or it does not, and the pronoun charge fails. Retreating to the creed abandons the pronoun as load-bearing, which concedes the stated thesis. Its one unsupported premise is empirical (F5). "Deserves its own sentence" is ornament; the logic beneath it is sound.

**Strongest objection to the thesis:** grant every grammatical rule and claim residual ambiguity — ordinary-language rules license a reading without fixing reference token by token, and the creed breaks the tie. The page's counters already exist: the naming rule ("When creatures share in an act, the Quran never hides them in a pronoun," line 625) and the 6:99 one-sentence shift ("He sent down, then We brought forth... the subject unchanged," line 667). The naming rule is an inductive universal over the book, and "Different hands cannot hide inside one sentence" answers clause-level editorial seams only by assertion. The page's strongest available reply, present but never gathered into one place, is burden reversal: the charge needs the plural to carry number, and every theologically neutral token (65:1, the mosques, the callers) testifies it does not. One sentence doing that explicitly would meet the objection at full strength.

# Council verdict — quran-we-he-i.html (post-revision)

## Seat 1 — First Principles: the three hatches

**(a) Creedal form (John 1:3 / Col 1:16 beyond the four tests): closed as an escape from this article's verdict; not refuted, and honestly not claimed to be.** Section 8 already states the boundary plainly: "the four tests cannot reach his form of the case. That is the honest boundary." The Final Verdict then converts the retreat into a concession: "A reader who abandons the pronoun and retreats to the creed... has conceded the pronoun case. That was the charge the polemic itself chose when it likened the Quran's We to Genesis 1:26." That is sound scoping, not overreach: the page's stated thesis is the pronoun charge in its two forms ("does We mean others help Allah" and "why the shifts"), so retreating to Nicaea abandons the load-bearing premise of that charge. What remains is a different article (the creedal case on its own ground), which the page correctly says "must be argued from there." Within the declared scope, genuinely closed; no pronoun article can close it further.

**(b) Pre-Islamic attestation of a strictly solitary royal we: materially weakened, with the residual honestly conceded rather than hidden.** The al-Farra chain does three distinct things. First, it dates the rule to d. 207 AH at the founding grammatical layer, so the rule is no longer a fifth-century Shi'i harmonization meeting the reader first at al-Tusi. Second, it exhibits the rule *inside the Quran at a theologically neutral verse*: 65:1, "the singular title of honor and the plural verb in one clause," which answers the circularity objection the page itself states best ("A rule read out of the Quran would explain the Quran perfectly and nothing else," line 545). Third, al-Farra glosses the divine Our itself ("plural in form and singular in meaning") and equates the creature's plural of 23:99 with "We created you before" (20:115), so the divine-We-as-majesty reading is attested at the earliest layer in both directions. Residual, and the page concedes it: the strictly solitary pre-Islamic we is still exhibited only through post-Quranic compilation ("Every human we on exhibit gathers rank around a speaker standing with his people"), and al-Farra is still two centuries after the book. The escape now requires discounting all post-Quranic grammar, which destroys the opponent's own Arabic philology. Weakened to a tolled position, not fully closed.

**(c) al-Khalil's reserve: closed as far as dated texts allow.** The reframe rests on checkable chronology: "The reserve predates the rule, and the rule answers the reserve. The founder paused over the parse, not the referent, and his own Kufan succession answered him within a generation" (line 427). Al-Khalil d. 170 AH, al-Farra d. 207 AH through al-Kisa'i's circle; "within a generation" is accurate. The reserve is scoped by al-Khalil's own stated reason ("because it is plural"). One wording outruns the quote slightly (finding F3 below). No textual escape remains; only the skeptic who discounts the whole grammatical tradition, which is hatch (b)'s tolled position again.

**What remains overall:** the token-ambiguity objection (Seat 2) and the strictly-solitary-we concession. Both are standing residuals of evidence, not defects of inference.

## Seat 2 — Reasoning

**The al-Farra chain is multi-link, not a single generalization.** "The Arabs use the plural verb for one person" (v3 p42) alone would *not* license "the divine We carries no number"; that is a second-person address construction generalizing to first person. But the page does not rest there: the 11:37 gloss is a direct statement on the divine first-person Our ("expressed in the plural while its meaning is singular"), and the 23:99 ↔ 20:115 equation puts creature-to-God plural and God's own We under one rule in one running comment. The chain holds.

**The 65:1 parallel holds as internal usage on al-Farra's stated reading, and that is its one dependency.** Correctly attributed ("The earliest commentary on the grammar of these verses counts no second speaker," line 466), but the mainstream alternative reading of talaqtum (the Prophet together with the community, the ruling generalized) is unengaged; on that reading the plural counts real referents and the neutral-exhibit force drops. One sentence acknowledging and weighing it would close the gap.

**The scope-catcher is an argument, not a device.** It is a dilemma: either the pronoun carries number, and then the four tests apply and "a method that convicts the Quran's We convicts Genesis first"; or it does not, and the pronoun charge fails. Retreating to the creed abandons the pronoun as load-bearing, which concedes the stated thesis. Its one unsupported premise is empirical (F5). "Deserves its own sentence" is ornament; the logic beneath it is sound.

**Strongest objection to the thesis:** grant every grammatical rule and claim residual ambiguity — ordinary-language rules license a reading without fixing reference token by token, and the creed breaks the tie. The page's counters already exist: the naming rule ("When creatures share in an act, the Quran never hides them in a pronoun," line 625) and the 6:99 one-sentence shift ("He sent down, then We brought forth... the subject unchanged," line 667). The naming rule is an inductive universal over the book, and "Different hands cannot hide inside one sentence" answers clause-level editorial seams only by assertion. The page's strongest available reply, present but never gathered into one place, is burden reversal: the charge needs the plural to carry number, and every theologically neutral token (65:1, the mosques, the callers) testifies it does not. One sentence doing that explicitly would meet the objection at full strength.
